newsitem.title: USA: Electric deregulation bill introduced in Texas.
newsitem.headline: Electric deregulation bill introduced in Texas.

text.p: Legislation to open the electric industry in Texas to retail competition and slash electric rates was introduced in the state legislature in Austin on Thursday.
Backed by independent power companies and large industrial customers, the bill calls for a 15 percent rate cut in September and retail competition on the Texas electric grid beginning in August 1998.

Introduced by State Senator Jerry Patterson of Pasadena and State Representative Mark Stiles of Beaumont, the bill would phase in retail competition over three years and require utilities to separate their transmission, generation and sales operations.
Schools and colleges would be able to choose electric suppliers by August 1, 1998, followed by residential customers on January 1, 1999 and industrial customers a year later.

The proposals met with stiff opposition from the state's largest electric utilities, who said the bill would threaten system reliability and prove a windfall for industrial customers and independent power marketers.

"The promise of a rate cut is a gimmick. Plain and simple, it is an attempt to gain support for this special-interest legislation," said Curtis Seidlits of the Association of Electric Companies of Texas, a utility trade group.
Utility lobbyists said the bill includes a loophole that would allow large industrial customers to move off the grid by buying a token stake in an independent power provider.

"It's a sweetheart deal for the industrial customers," said Bruce Gibson, Houston Industries' senior vice president for governmental affairs. "This would be a huge windfall for industrial customers if they pass this bill."

Spurred on by promises of up to 40 percent savings on electric rates, high-cost states like California and New Hampshire are leading the charge to break up electric monopolies and open the electric grid to competition.
The deregulation issue sparks heated debates in Texas, home to energy marketers like Enron Corp, NGC Corp and PanEnergy Corp that are positioned to become national electric companies.
The state legislature, which meets every two years, in the 1995 session adopted a bill allowing wholesale competition and a study of retail competition in other states by 1999.

"Texas is becoming the center for this industry. For Texas to be seen as late in deregulating would be crazy," Jeff Skilling, Enron's president, said. Skilling said Texans would save an estimated $4 billion a year off a $16 billion a year electric bill once the market is open to competition.

Gov. George Bush has called on the legislature to study options for opening the grid to competition, but supporters said the deregulation bill faced an "uphill battle" to pass the state Senate during the legislative session that runs through May.
"Competition is coming," Stiles said. "The question is when and under what authority. I would rather pass a bill in the state legislature than have the federal government dictate how we get there."
Texas electric rates are among the lowest in the country, but Texans' electric bills are among the highest, in large part because of summer air conditioning demand.
